title: The effect of parenting interventions to support language and literacy development in 3-7-year-old children in low- and middle-income countries: Systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Children in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) often have limited access to the structured home learning experiences that support language and literacy development during the critical years around school entry. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of parenting interventions targeting children's language or literacy in these settings. Twenty-six experimental and quasi-experimental studies from 15 countries involving 6,264 children aged 3-7 were included. Dependent effect sizes were synthesized using random-effects models with robust variance estimation. Parenting interventions were found to be associated with positive pooled effects on language (k = 21, g = 1.35, 95% CI [0.62, 2.09]) and literacy (k = 19, g = 0.94, 95% CI [0.56, 1.33]). Estimates were similar when restricted to the subset of 23 randomized controlled trials. Heterogeneity was substantial for both child outcomes. Exploratory moderator analyses suggested larger effects for both language and literacy in contexts with morphosyllabic script and, for literacy, in interventions that included shared book reading. Risk of bias was judged to be moderate, principally because most studies lacked prespecified analysis plans. We conclude that parenting interventions can support early language and literacy development in LMICs, although some uncertainty remains concerning the magnitude of effects, especially for language.
